Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro — I'm Avery, I'll run through the high level and Samir will jump into the tech bits.
[00:12] Jordan Meyers: Great, thanks. We're mainly here to validate that the private deployment meets our sec reqs — we have a couple of lines for SOC2 and an audit in Q1.
[00:21] Priya Rao: Also want to confirm KMS pathing — we use an external HSM provider and need to ensure key import/export constraints.
[00:28] Samir Patel: Awesome, yep. We'll go through network diagrams and then deep dive on seccomp and egress. Quick note, the transcript may have some mis-heard terms, like KV cash instead of KV cache.
[00:37] Meera Singhal: That's fine, as long as we can get the artifacts.
[00:40] Avery Chen: Cool. We'll start with topology. Nina, can you pull up the simplified private layout?
[00:46] Nina Lopez: Sure, quick share. So the pattern we recommend is split control plane and data plane. Control plane sits in customer VPC but we provide a narrow management channel to Redwood's control endpoints — optional air-gapped control plane if you want full on-prem. Data plane nodes are inside the private subnet with no public IPs.
[01:02] Luis Velasquez: When you say "narrow management channel" is that just outbound HTTPS over 443 to your endpoints? We need to know IPs for our firewall team.
[01:12] Samir Patel: Yes, outbound-only. We supply an allowlist of range(s) — we support fixed egress IPs for Dedicated and for Private we provide a stable set of endpoints. We'll send a csv with the exact CIDRs.
[01:25] Priya Rao: For the private on-prem package we need static endpoints; dynamic DNS changing mid-audit is a non-starter.
[01:33] Avery Chen: Understood — we have a stable range option and can pin to your tenancy.
[01:38] Jordan Meyers: Next — egress. We have a strict rule: no outbound to general internet except via approved proxy. How does Redwood handle egress for model downloads and telemetry?
[01:50] Samir Patel: Good question. There are two patterns:
[01:53] - Model/cache pulls can be staged via an internal artifact repository you control — we support pulling from private S3, Git LFS, or an airgapped tarball you ship.
[02:02] - Telemetry and metrics can be forwarded to your telemetry endpoints; we can disable outbound telemetry entirely. If enabled, it's proxied via your egress proxy so it follows your egress inspection.
[02:12] Meera Singhal: So we can route logs to our Splunk and ensure no plaintext goes out?
[02:17] Samir Patel: Yes — log forwarding supports TLS to your collector and we can use mutual TLS if required.
[02:22] Priya Rao: About egress filtering: do you support seccomp or system-level sandboxing to limit kernel syscalls in the inference runtime? We've seen noisy containers cause attack surface concerns.
[02:35] Samir Patel: We run inference in a process-isolated runtime. For the on-prem package we offer kernel hardening: seccomp filters, AppArmor profiles, and optional user namespaces. We can provide the profile examples. Note: some of the seccomp rules need tuning depending on quantized kernels, e.g., if a kernel uses shared memory syscalls they must be allowed.
[02:57] Luis Velasquez: Any chance the seccomp blocks will break model ops? We have some custom ops for our vector quant.
[03:04] Samir Patel: It can, yeah. That's why our sandboxing is conservative by default; we recommend a staging pass where we run workload traces and generate an allowlist. We can share our trace-run script.
[03:16] Jordan Meyers: Let's talk KMS. We prefer to bring our own keys in an external HSM (Thales). Is there a path to integrate?
[03:24] Nina Lopez: Yes — we support external KMS via the standard KMIP/PKCS11 flows or cloud KMS providers. For HSMs like Thales you can either expose an endpoint inside the VPC or we integrate via a trusted gateway. Keys never leave the HSM.
[03:36] Priya Rao: Rotation policy — can Redwood rotate CMKs on our behalf or must we rotate externally?
[03:41] Samir Patel: We can orchestrate rotation but for BYOK we typically leave rotation to the customer's KMS. We will support automatic re-wrap of envelopes if you want Redwood to rotate envelope keys, but the root CMK stays in your control.
[03:53] Meera Singhal: For audit evidence, do you generate key use logs with KMS request IDs? We need to tie model inference calls to key access events for forensics.
[04:02] Samir Patel: Absolutely — we emit KMS request IDs in the audit trail and you can forward those logs to your SIEM alongside the platform audit logs. We also keep non-repudiable event chains with timestamps.
[04:12] Priya Rao: About RBAC and SSO — our org uses SAML SSO via Okta and SCIM for provisioning. Can you support just-in-time provisioning and granular roles?
[04:23] Avery Chen: Yes — Redwood supports SAML and OIDC for SSO, SCIM for provisioning users and groups, and fine-grained RBAC with role templates. You can map Okta groups to project-level roles.
[04:34] Jordan Meyers: For compliance, we need to demonstrate separation of duties — can you show role audit logs, changes to access, and log exports?
[04:44] Samir Patel: We provide an audit log API and daily exports. The control plane audit includes identity events, role changes, and API key activity. For Private we provide local audit relays so logs stay inside your environment.
[04:57] Luis Velasquez: When you say "local audit relays" — are those sidecar collectors? How do we prevent tampering if an attacker gains root on a node?
[05:06] Nina Lopez: Good point. We recommend a multi-tier approach: immutable syslog forwarding to a hardened collector VM, signed log chains (append-only), and optional remote write to an external write-once storage. For tamper evidence we support signing events with a key stored in your HSM.
[05:22] Meera Singhal: That would satisfy auditors.
[05:25] Priya Rao: A nit: does the on-prem package require kernel module installs or privileged containers? Our security baseline forbids privileged containers.
[05:33] Samir Patel: The runtime can run unprivileged. We avoid privileged containers unless you opt into node-level GPU drivers that need device plugin privileges; in that case we provide a separate GPU host pool and limit privileges to the host driver install process.
[05:49] Jordan Meyers: Can you walk through an incident scenario — exfiltration via model prompt output? How do we detect and block sensitive egress?
[05:59] Avery Chen: Sure. We have several controls: prefix/KV caching to reduce external calls, output filters for PII regex/rules, and the ability to scrub or redact outputs before they're returned. Also, egress proxies provide DLP rules; you can run model output through a DLP pipeline.
[06:14] Luis Velasquez: Are the output filters run in-line or async? Latency sensitive for inference.
[06:19] Samir Patel: We support both. For strict controls we run in-line with a lightweight rule engine. For large-scale throughput, we suggest async scanning and blocking on policy violations via a fast reject path — depends on your latency SLOs.
[06:32] Priya Rao: Regarding data residency — we will have EU-only training and inference for some workloads. Can you guarantee that model artifacts and logs stay in the EU VPC?
[06:41] Nina Lopez: Yes — you can pin region and we will ensure artifacts are stored on EU-resident storage. For Private, it's inside your VPC so residency is controlled by your network boundaries.
[06:51] Jordan Meyers: A few quick questions from Compliance: do you have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001?
[06:58] Avery Chen: We do have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001. I'll share the latest reports under NDA — link will be provided.
[07:04] Meera Singhal: Please include evidence around change management and vulnerability scanning cadence.
[07:08] Samir Patel: We run quarterly pentests and continuous vuln scans; we can provide scan summaries and remediation timelines.
[07:14] Priya Rao: On telemetry — we need to ensure no model weights or unencrypted token logs leave our environment.
[07:20] Samir Patel: By default model weights never leave your storage. Telemetry is configurable and can be disabled; if enabled, sensitive fields are redacted.
[07:28] Luis Velasquez: Regarding firewall rules, can you drop traffic at kernel level for suspicious flows? We want defense-in-depth.
[07:36] Samir Patel: Yes — we recommend host-level firewalling plus egress proxy and network ACLs. For on-prem we supply iptables/ufw templates and can support nftables if that's your stack.
[07:48] Jordan Meyers: Ok, let's capture next steps.
[07:51] Avery Chen: Recap — we'll send SOC2/ISO docs, share the egress CIDR allowlist, provide seccomp/AppArmor profile examples and the trace script, and schedule the KMS workshop. Anything else?
[08:05] Priya Rao: Please include the sample iptables and example for mutal TLS with our Splunk collector.
[08:11] Samir Patel: We'll include a sample mTLS config and the scripted audit-forwarder.
[08:16] Meera Singhal: Can we get an onboarding timeline? We are targeting a pilot in mid-November.
[08:21] Avery Chen: We'll aim for pilot readiness by 2027-11-15. Samir and Priya to coordinate on exact dates.
[08:26] Jordan Meyers: Great, thanks all.
[08:29] Luis Velasquez: Thanks.
[08:30] [crosstalk]
[08:33] Meeting end summary (voice): next steps reiterated, action owners assigned, schedule follow-up for KMS workshop.
